name: Domain of discourse
quick: The collection of objects a quantified variable may represent.
definition: A domain fixes the allowed values before we evaluate a predicate or quantified statement. Different variables can have different domains, such as requests and workers. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, domains in this lesson are nonempty.
example: $\exists x\,(x^2=2)$ is false over the integers and true over the real numbers.
confusion: Changing the domain changes the claim, even when the formula looks identical. This use of domain is related to, but not identical with, the domain of a function.

name: Predicate
quick: A property or relationship with inputs, which becomes a proposition when those inputs are specified.
definition: A predicate names a condition to be tested on its domain. A one-input predicate describes a property; a two-input predicate can describe a relationship. Its truth can depend on the supplied inputs.
example: For integers, define $P(x)$ to mean $x>5$. Then $P(8)$ is true and $P(5)$ is false.
confusion: A predicate with unspecified free inputs need not yet have a single truth value.

name: Argument of a predicate
quick: An input supplied to a predicate.
definition: The arguments occupy ordered input positions. In $R(x,y)$, the first position receives $x$ and the second receives $y$. Substitution must preserve these positions.
example: If $R(x,y)$ means $x<y$, then $R(2,7)$ is true while $R(7,2)$ is false.
confusion: Here argument means input, not a logical argument consisting of premises and a conclusion.

name: Quantifier
quick: An instruction saying whether every allowed object or at least one allowed object must satisfy a condition.
definition: Universal quantification uses $\forall$ for every allowed value. Existential quantification uses $\exists$ for at least one. A quantifier controls occurrences of its variable in a specified part of the formula, its scope.
example: $\forall n\in\mathbb Z,\ n^2\geq0$ says that every integer has a nonnegative square.
confusion: Quantifiers do not determine a domain by themselves; say what their variables are allowed to represent.

name: Universal quantification
quick: A claim that every object in the stated domain satisfies a condition.
definition: $\forall x\in D,\ P(x)$ holds exactly when each allowed value of $x$ makes $P(x)$ true. One failing allowed value is a counterexample. An exhaustive finite check can establish such a claim; a finite sample cannot establish it for all integers.
example: $\forall n\in\mathbb Z,\ n^2>0$ is false: $n=0$ gives a counterexample.
confusion: A value outside the domain cannot refute the claim.

name: Existential quantification
quick: A claim that at least one object in the stated domain satisfies a condition.
definition: $\exists x\in D,\ P(x)$ holds when some allowed object makes $P(x)$ true. Establish it by exhibiting such an object and verifying its property; refuting it requires excluding every allowed object.
example: $\exists n\in\mathbb Z,\ n^2=9$ is true because $n=3$ is an integer and $3^2=9$.
confusion: At least one does not mean exactly one: $-3$ works too.

name: Witness
quick: An allowed object that makes the predicate in an existential claim true.
definition: A witness supplies the example promised by “there exists.” To use one, check both that it lies in the required domain and that it satisfies the condition. In nested quantifiers, the witness may depend on choices made before its quantifier.
example: For $\exists n\in\mathbb Z,\ n^2=9$, either 3 or $-3$ is a witness.
confusion: One failed candidate does not show that no witness exists.

name: Scope of a quantifier
quick: The part of a formula controlled by a quantifier.
definition: Parentheses or an explicitly stated convention identify the expression to which a quantifier applies. Its variable occurrences inside that expression are bound by it, unless a nearer quantifier controls them.
example: In $(\forall x\,P(x))\land Q(x)$, the first quantifier governs $P(x)$ but not $Q(x)$.
confusion: Repeating the same letter outside the scope does not extend the quantifier.
section: Scope, free variables, and bound variables

name: Free variable occurrence
quick: A variable occurrence not controlled by a quantifier in the formula.
definition: A free occurrence needs a supplied value if we are to evaluate the formula as a proposition. Freedom belongs to occurrences: the same letter may have both free and bound occurrences in one expression.
example: In $(\forall x\,P(x))\land Q(x)$, the $x$ in $Q(x)$ is free.
confusion: Do not decide from the letter alone; check its position and the quantifier scopes.

name: Bound variable occurrence
quick: A variable occurrence controlled by a quantifier whose scope includes it.
definition: Binding tells us how the occurrence ranges over its domain. Consistently renaming a bound variable preserves meaning only when the rename preserves which quantifier controls each occurrence.
example: Both inputs in $\forall x\,(P(x)\to Q(x))$ are bound by the displayed universal quantifier.
confusion: Blindly renaming a letter can accidentally bind a formerly free occurrence.
section: Scope, free variables, and bound variables

name: Variable capture
quick: Accidentally making a formerly free occurrence bound when renaming or substituting.
definition: A safe bound-variable rename preserves the binding structure. A fresh name unused in the formula avoids accidental capture and confusion with inner quantifiers.
example: Renaming $x$ to $y$ in $\forall x\,R(x,y)$ produces $\forall y\,R(y,y)$ and incorrectly binds the formerly free input $y$. Use $\forall t\,R(t,y)$ instead.
confusion: A rename must preserve meanings, not just replace matching letters.
section: Scope, free variables, and bound variables

name: Open formula
quick: A formula with at least one free variable occurrence.
definition: Its truth may still depend on a value assigned to a free variable, even after the domain and predicate meanings are fixed.
example: $\exists x\,R(x,y)$ is open because $y$ is free.
confusion: Having some quantifiers does not necessarily make the formula closed.
section: Scope, free variables, and bound variables

name: Closed formula
quick: A formula with no free variable occurrences.
definition: Once its domain and predicate meanings are fixed, a closed formula has a truth value without further input assignments.
example: $\forall x\exists y\,R(x,y)$ is closed; both input occurrences are bound.
confusion: Closed means free of unspecified variable occurrences, not automatically true.
section: Scope, free variables, and bound variables

name: Quantifier order
quick: The left-to-right order that determines which choices can depend on earlier ones.
definition: In $\forall x\exists y\,R(x,y)$, the chosen witness $y$ may depend on the given $x$. In $\exists y\forall x\,R(x,y)$, one fixed $y$ must work for every $x$. Two adjacent quantifiers of the same kind may be swapped without changing meaning.
example: Over integers, $\forall x\exists y\,(y>x)$ is true using $y=x+1$. The reversed claim is false because no integer exceeds itself.
confusion: Permission for a witness to depend on an input does not force actual dependence: sometimes one witness works for everyone.

name: Uniqueness
quick: The condition that at most one object satisfies the required property.
definition: Uniqueness rules out two distinct solutions. Exactly one combines existence with uniqueness: show that a solution exists and that every solution equals it.
example: $n+3=5$ has exactly one integer solution: 2 works, and rearranging forces $n=2$.
confusion: No solutions satisfies at most one, but fails exactly one.

name: Vacuous truth
quick: Truth of a universal claim because there is no allowed counterexample, often because its condition is never met.
definition: $\forall x(P(x)\to Q(x))$ is true if no object satisfies $P$: each implication has a false antecedent. A universal claim over an empty domain is also true because no domain element violates it.
example: “Every file larger than 1 GB is archived” is true when there are no files larger than 1 GB.
confusion: Vacuous truth makes no existence claim. An existential claim over an empty domain is false.

name: Universal instantiation
quick: Applying a universal statement to a particular allowed object.
definition: From $\forall x\in D,\ P(x)$ and $a\in D$, infer $P(a)$. The general statement covers this instance because the object belongs to the specified domain.
example: If every book on a shelf is catalogued, a particular book on that shelf is catalogued.
confusion: The conclusion is not licensed for an object outside the domain.

name: Existential introduction
quick: Inferring that an example exists from a verified allowed example.
definition: From $P(a)$ and $a\in D$, infer $\exists x\in D,\ P(x)$. Naming the witness is stronger information than the existence conclusion.
example: After checking that 12 is an integer divisible by 6, conclude that some integer is divisible by 6.
confusion: The reverse move is invalid for a previously chosen object: existence does not tell you that your favorite candidate works.

name: Universal generalization
quick: Proving a universal claim by reasoning about an arbitrary allowed object without extra special assumptions.
definition: Choose an arbitrary element of the domain and establish the predicate using only hypotheses that apply to every such element. Then the proof covers the whole domain.
example: Let $n$ be an arbitrary integer. Since $n+1$ is an integer greater than $n$, every integer has a larger integer.
confusion: Checking selected values is not generalization over an infinite domain.

name: Arbitrary object
quick: An allowed object with no special properties beyond the stated assumptions.
definition: Reasoning about an arbitrary object must work regardless of which allowed object was supplied. The proof may use its domain membership and stated hypotheses but cannot silently choose a convenient special value.
example: An arbitrary integer $n$ may be negative, zero, or positive. A proof cannot assume $n>0$ unless this is part of the claim or a separately justified case.
confusion: A specially chosen witness and an arbitrary input play different logical roles.
section: Scope, free variables, and bound variables

name: Countermodel
quick: A domain and interpretation making all premises true and the proposed conclusion false.
definition: A countermodel refutes validity of a quantified inference by specifying the objects and exactly when each predicate holds. One such interpretation is enough.
example: On $D=\{a,b\}$, let $P$ hold only at $b$. Then $\exists xP(x)$ is true while $P(a)$ is false.
confusion: Simply making the conclusion false is insufficient if a premise is also false.

name: ∀ — for every
quick: Read “for every” allowed value of the following variable.
definition: In $\forall x\in D,\ P(x)$, the quantifier ranges $x$ over $D$ and requires $P(x)$ for every such value. Parentheses specify its scope in larger formulas.
example: $\forall n\in\mathbb Z,\ n^2\geq0$: “for every integer n, n squared is nonnegative.”
confusion: This symbol does not say there is exactly one value, nor that the domain is nonempty.

name: ∃ — there exists
quick: Read “there exists at least one” allowed value.
definition: In $\exists x\in D,\ P(x)$, at least one value from $D$ must satisfy the predicate. The value is called a witness.
example: $\exists n\in\mathbb Z,\ n^2=9$: “there exists an integer n whose square is nine.”
confusion: It does not assert exactly one witness.

name: ∃! — there exists exactly one
quick: Read “there exists exactly one.”
definition: $\exists!x\,P(x)$ asserts existence of a witness and equality of every other witness to that same object.
example: $\exists!n\in\mathbb Z,\ n+3=5$ holds because the only solution is 2.
confusion: The exclamation mark expresses uniqueness; it is not negation here.

name: ∈ — is an element of
quick: Read “is an element of” or “belongs to.”
definition: $x\in D$ asserts that the object $x$ belongs to the collection $D$. In a quantified expression it specifies the allowed domain.
example: $3\in\mathbb Z$ says that 3 is an integer.
confusion: Membership relates an object to a collection. Containment of one set in another is a different relation, taught in Sets.

name: ℤ — integers
quick: All whole-number values, including negatives and zero.
definition: $\mathbb Z=\{\ldots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\ldots\}$ denotes the integers.
example: $-3\in\mathbb Z$ but $1/2\notin\mathbb Z$.
confusion: An integer domain excludes nonintegral real numbers, even when they solve the displayed equation.

name: ℕ₀ — nonnegative integers
quick: The integers 0, 1, 2, and so on.
definition: $\mathbb N_0$ explicitly includes zero. Stating the subscript avoids the differing conventions sometimes used for natural numbers.
example: $\forall n\in\mathbb N_0,\ n\geq0$ is true.
confusion: Do not silently use positive integers when zero is allowed; zero often decides a quantified claim.

name: ℝ — real numbers
quick: The numbers on the ordinary number line.
definition: The real numbers include integers, fractions, and irrational values such as $\sqrt2$. A real domain can therefore supply witnesses unavailable in an integer domain.
example: $\sqrt2\in\mathbb R$ and $(\sqrt2)^2=2$.
confusion: The real numbers do not include a square root of $-1$.

name: ∅ — empty set
quick: The collection containing no elements.
definition: $D=\varnothing$ says that the domain has no objects. A universal claim over it has no counterexample; an existential claim over it has no witness.
example: There is no $x\in\varnothing$, so $\exists x\in\varnothing,\ x=x$ is false.
confusion: The empty collection is different from a collection containing the number zero.
